ety.text: From Middle English future, futur, from Old French futur, from Latin futūrus, irregular future active participle of sum (“to be”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰuH- (“to become, be”). Cognate with Old English bēo (“to become, will be; to be”). More at be. Doublet of futur. Displaced native Old English tōweard, which took on a different meaning as toward, and Middle English afterhede (“future”, literally “afterhood”) in the given sense.

senses.d: The time ahead; those moments yet to be experienced.
Something that will happen in moments yet to come.
Goodness in what is yet to come. Something to look forward to.
ex: There is no future in dwelling on the past.

senses.d: The likely prospects for or fate of someone or something in time to come.
ex: Again, it's unlikely they will return to traffic, but futures have been secured for four that will be heading to heritage railways [...].

senses.d: Verb tense used to talk about events that will happen in the future; future tense.
An object that retrieves the value of a promise.
Having to do with or occurring in the future.
ex: Future generations will either laugh or cry at our stupidity.
It[The study] also attempts to predict the future progression of AI as it relates to new inventions.
